what: Selective Insurance writes property and casualty insurance for businesses, and some personal insurance. Its policies cover commercial buildings, vehicles, workers’ compensation and liability, sold exclusively through independent insurance agents in the eastern and midwestern United States.
customers: Small and mid-sized businesses, public entities such as school districts and municipalities, and homeowners, all reached through a network of independent agency partners rather than direct sales.
money: Property, general liability, commercial auto and workers’ compensation for businesses.
Homeowners and auto insurance, plus excess and surplus lines for harder-to-place risks.
moat: Selective’s distinctive asset is the depth of its relationships with a deliberately limited number of independent agents, who are treated as partners and given technology and underwriting support. That focus gets it a first look at good business in its territories. Its long record of underwriting profitably, rather than buying growth with cheap pricing, is the thing that compounds in insurance.
risks: Commercial auto and liability losses have run above expectations across the industry, driven by larger jury awards, and reserves set years ago can prove insufficient.
Seven analysts average a $104.57 target against a $102.71 price — essentially no upside, which is a meaningful signal from a group that rarely publishes flat targets.
Geographic concentration in the eastern United States means a single severe storm season affects an outsized share of the book.
Insurance pricing is cyclical, and after several years of rate increases the market is softening as capital flows in.
Debt of $1.0B against $18.0M of cash looks stark, though an insurer’s liquidity sits in its investment portfolio rather than in cash.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year shown, from $3.4B in 2021 to $5.3B in 2025.
Investment income rises as the bond portfolio rolls into higher yields, and that income arrives regardless of underwriting results.
The shares trade at about 12.3 times earnings, in line with the sector for a company with a better-than-average record.
Free cash flow of about $1.1B reflects premiums collected ahead of claims paid, which is the float that makes insurance attractive when underwriting is disciplined.
watch: The combined ratio, and reserve development on prior years. The first says whether this year’s policies are profitable; the second says whether previous years’ were, and in casualty insurance the second surprises people far more often.
view: Insurance looks complicated and reduces to two questions. Did you charge enough for the risks you took, and did you set aside enough for the claims you have not yet paid? The first shows up in the combined ratio within a year. The second can take a decade, which is why insurers that look wonderful sometimes turn out not to have been. Any serious view on Selective has to engage with both, and the second is where the current worry sits.

The industry-wide problem is casualty — commercial auto and general liability — where jury awards have grown faster than anyone’s reserving assumptions. Policies written five or seven years ago were priced for a world where a serious injury claim settled for less than it now does. Every carrier in this market is working through that, and the reserves set in those years are being topped up across the sector. Selective is not exempt, and that is the single biggest thing to watch here.

Set against it, this is a genuinely well-run underwriter. The business model — a deliberately limited number of independent agents, treated as partners and supported with technology — gets Selective a first look at good business in its territories rather than the leftovers, and its long record is one of underwriting profitably rather than buying growth with cheap pricing. In insurance that distinction is everything, because growing fast in a soft market is the standard way these companies destroy themselves.

At 12.3 times earnings the price is ordinary for the sector, and the seven analysts seeing essentially no upside are telling you the same thing I would: this is a fair price for a good company at an awkward point in the cycle. The genuine tailwind nobody talks about is investment income — the bond portfolio keeps rolling into higher yields, and that income arrives whether or not underwriting cooperates. I would own this for the quality of the underwriting culture and I would read the reserve development disclosure before anything else in every report.
bull: Reserve additions prove adequate, rate increases earn through, and investment income on a bond portfolio rolling into higher yields lifts earnings on an unchanged book.
bear: Casualty reserves set in the soft years prove badly short while a softening market makes it impossible to price the shortfall back, and several years of earnings go to fixing the past.
